subject: Public health
summary: The interquartile range (IQR) measures spread of middle 50% of data, useful for summarizing health metrics and detecting outliers. It helps clinicians assess variability in populations.

sections.p: IQR is the difference between the 75th (Q3) and 25th (Q1) percentiles of a dataset. It captures central dispersion, ignoring extreme values.
IQR itself has no severity scale, but a wide IQR indicates high variability in a health outcome, suggesting heterogeneous risk or intervention effects.

High IQR in health data often reflects underlying heterogeneity: differing socioeconomic status, access to care, comorbidities, or measurement error. In low-resource settings, factors like malaria prevalence or nutrition gaps widen IQR.
Clinically, a wide IQR in, for example, blood pressure readings across a clinic indicates inconsistent control, prompting review of treatment protocols.
Use descriptive statistics to calculate IQR from raw data. When data are skewed, IQR is preferred over standard deviation.

t.b: Calculates Q1, Q3, and IQR; answers: what is the spread of central data? Result: numeric IQR value indicating variability
Assesses outliers and errors; answers: are extreme values genuine? Result: improved accuracy of IQR

sections.p: A very large IQR may mask subgroups with poor outcomes; it can delay identification of high-risk patients.
Address sources of variability: standardize measurement protocols, improve access to care, and tailor interventions to subgroups. Monitor IQR over time to assess program effectiveness.
Recalculate IQR after interventions to evaluate reduction in variability. Use IQR trends to guide resource allocation in low-resource settings.
Standard deviation (SD) measures overall spread, including extremes, while IQR focuses on middle 50%.
If data are heavily skewed, IQR may underestimate true variability. Small sample sizes can produce unstable quartiles.

faq.q: Why use IQR instead of standard deviation?
faq.a: IQR is less affected by extreme values, giving a clearer picture of typical variability in skewed data.

faq.q: Can IQR be used for binary outcomes?
faq.a: No, IQR applies to continuous data; for binary outcomes use proportions or odds ratios.

faq.q: How often should IQR be recalculated in a program?
faq.a: At least annually, or after major protocol changes, to track variability trends.

exam: Explain how IQR helps identify heterogeneity in a population health study.
Compare and contrast IQR with standard deviation in the context of a skewed dataset.
Describe steps to reduce a wide IQR in a low-resource clinic setting.
